title: Keeping the Camp Clean: Impurity, Restitution, and Jealousy
summary: Three laws protect the camp where God dwells. People with certain skin diseases, bodily discharges, or contact with a corpse are sent outside it; a person who wrongs a neighbor must confess, repay in full plus a fifth, and bring an offering; and a husband who suspects his wife of adultery with no witness must bring her before the LORD for a solemn oath and a drink of bitter water, leaving the verdict to God.
story: Chapters 1 to 4 arranged the camp around the tabernacle. Chapters 5 and 6 turn from the camp's shape to its condition. If God lives in the middle of Israel, then what happens anywhere in the camp matters to him, whether a physical impurity, a wrong done to a neighbor, or a secret betrayal inside a marriage. The three laws here move inward: from the whole camp, to relationships between neighbors, to the hidden life of one household. Each ends with the camp, the neighbor, or the marriage restored or judged in God's presence. The book is preparing a holy people to travel with a holy God, and it wants readers to see that holiness reaches into places no one else can see.
historical:
Like the rest of Numbers 1 to 10, these laws are set at Sinai before the departure. The restitution law restates and extends Leviticus 6:1-7, and the impurity rules assume the detailed laws of Leviticus 13 to 15. What is new here is the application to the camp as the place where God dwells, the explicit requirement of confession, and the case of a wronged person who has died with no relative to receive payment.

The jealousy ritual has parallels in ancient Near Eastern law. The Code of Hammurabi, from Babylon around 1750 BC, provides that a wife accused by her husband without proof may clear herself by an oath, and that a wife accused by others must submit to the river ordeal, plunging into the river so that the river god could judge her. An innocent woman could drown in such a test. The Israelite procedure takes place at the sanctuary and uses water, dust, and ink, which could harm no one by themselves; any verdict had to come from God. The Mishnah, the rabbinic law code compiled around AD 200, contains a whole tractate on the rite and records that it was discontinued in the first century AD.
cultural:
The three conditions that required a person to leave the camp were skin disease (Hebrew tsaraat, traditionally translated leprosy, though it covered a range of conditions and was not limited to what is now called Hansen's disease), bodily discharges, and contact with the dead. None of them is a sin. They are conditions associated with death and the breakdown of the body, and the God of life could not have them in his dwelling. Exclusion was painful but usually temporary, and the laws of Leviticus provided for washing and return.

Marriage in ancient Israel gave the husband legal authority over his wife, and suspicion of adultery was dangerous for her. With no witness, there was no trial; a jealous husband and his relatives might take matters into their own hands. The ritual moves the case out of the household and into the presence of God. The priest loosens the woman's hair, a sign of shame or mourning also required of the diseased (Leviticus 13:45); she holds a plain barley offering with no oil or incense, like the sin offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:11), because it calls iniquity to mind; she swears an oath and answers “Amen, Amen”; and the written curse is washed into the water she drinks. The words become part of what she takes into herself.
literary: The chapter is three laws of unequal length, each introduced by the formula “And the LORD said to Moses” or its variant. A single word ties the last two together. The person who wrongs a neighbor “acts unfaithfully against the LORD” (verse 6), and the suspected wife is one who “is unfaithful to him” (verse 12); both use the Hebrew verb for breach of trust. Wronging a neighbor is betraying God, and a hidden betrayal in a marriage is the kind of unfaithfulness God also knows from his people. The jealousy law itself is repetitive and circling, returning three times to the bitter water, the curse, and the swelling and shriveling, and closing with a summary (verses 29-31) in the style of other priestly rulings. The repetition slows the reader and gives the rite its gravity.

outline.t: The unclean sent outside the camp where God dwells
Confession and restitution for wrongs against others
A husband's suspicion and the offering of jealousy
The bitter water and its outcome
Summary of the law of jealousy

doctrines.note: The reason for sending the unclean out is stated in verse 3: the camp is the place “where I dwell among them.” Holiness is not an abstract standard; it follows from God's presence, and it reaches the body, the neighbor, and the marriage bed.

Verse 7 requires the guilty person to confess the sin and repay in full, adding a fifth. Repentance in Scripture is not only a feeling or even only words to God; it includes putting right what was taken from the person who was wronged.
The jealousy law places a hidden matter before God, who sees what no witness saw. Its effect is to take judgment out of the hands of a suspicious husband and leave it with the LORD.

words.note: Shakan, to dwell or settle. Verse 3 grounds the whole chapter in it: the camp is where God dwells among his people. From the same root comes mishkan, the tabernacle, and later Jewish writers used the related word Shekinah for God's dwelling presence. The laws exist because God has chosen to live close by.

Maal, to act unfaithfully, to break trust. It describes both the one who wrongs a neighbor, which is counted as unfaithfulness to the LORD (verse 6), and the wife who betrays her husband (verses 12 and 27). Elsewhere it is used for Israel's betrayal of God through idolatry, so it connects marriage and covenant.

Qinah, jealousy or zeal. It is the passionate protectiveness of a person who will not share what is rightfully his. In a husband it can be justified or groundless, and verse 14 allows for both. The same word describes God's own jealousy for his people (Exodus 34:14), which is not insecurity but the love of a spouse who refuses to be replaced.

christ: The three conditions of verse 2 read like a list of the people Jesus met in the Gospels. A leper knelt before him, and “Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man” (Mark 1:41); a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years touched his cloak and was healed (Mark 5:25-29); and he took a dead girl by the hand and raised her (Mark 5:41). Under the law, touching these people made a person unclean. With Jesus, the direction reverses: his touch makes them clean. The restitution law finds an echo in Zacchaeus, who, on meeting Jesus, promised, “if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). And the jealousy of verse 14 belongs to the larger biblical picture of God as a husband to his people, which Paul applies to the church: “I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy” (2 Corinthians 11:2). These are thematic connections, not predictions, but they show where the chapter's concerns lead.

hard.q: Isn't the jealousy ritual unfair to women, since there is no test for a suspected husband?
hard.a: The asymmetry is real. The law assumes a society in which a husband held legal authority over his wife, and it gives no parallel procedure for a wife who suspects her husband. Some scholars read the rite chiefly as an instrument of male control, putting a woman through public humiliation on the basis of a feeling. Others, while granting the patriarchal setting, argue that its effect was protective. Without witnesses, there could be no human verdict; the penalty for proven adultery was death for both parties (Leviticus 20:10); and a suspicious husband might otherwise act violently on his own. The rite admits that the husband may be wrong (verse 14), takes the case away from him, and uses harmless ingredients, so that an innocent woman is publicly cleared and able to conceive (verse 28). Unlike the Babylonian river ordeal, it could not kill an innocent person by accident. Readers can hold both observations together: the law works within the structures of its world, and it limits the damage those structures could do.

questions: Verse 6 counts a wrong done to a neighbor as unfaithfulness to the LORD. How would it change your view of an apology to see it that way?
Restitution in this law includes an extra fifth. What does it look like to repay more than the bare minimum when you have wronged someone?
The jealousy law takes a hidden suspicion and places it before God rather than in the husband's hands. What suspicions or grievances do you need to hand over rather than act on?
